```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  fromJSON(paste(txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = TRUE)
}

us_mod <- read_json5_clean("united_states_post_independence.json5")
us_sett <- fromJSON("united_states_post_independence_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
diag_na <- fromJSON("../../_shared/sites_northern_america/config/kriging_diagnostics.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
diag_hp <- fromJSON("../../_shared/sites_hawaii_polynesia/config/kriging_diagnostics.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
hl <- us_mod$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark

interp_reg <- function (arg0_reg, arg1_yr) {
  p <- arg0_reg$population
  ys <- as.character(arg1_yr)
  if (!is.null(p[[ys]])) return(as.numeric(p[[ys]]))
  ks <- sort(as.integer(names(p)))
  if (length(ks) == 0 || arg1_yr < ks[1]) return(0)
  if (arg1_yr > ks[length(ks)]) return(as.numeric(p[[as.character(ks[length(ks)])]]))
  k0 <- max(ks[ks <= arg1_yr])
  k1 <- min(ks[ks >= arg1_yr])
  if (k0 == k1) return(as.numeric(p[[as.character(k0)]]))
  v0 <- as.numeric(p[[as.character(k0)]])
  v1 <- as.numeric(p[[as.character(k1)]])
  round(v0 + (v1 - v0) * (arg1_yr - k0) / (k1 - k0))
}
```

# Abstract

Between the Treaty of Paris in 1783AD and 2026AD, the combined population of the 50 U.S. states, the District of Columbia, Bermuda and post-1898AD American Samoa multiplied nearly seventy-nine-fold (78,78x) from `r viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["1783"]])` (4.375.088) to `r viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["2026"]])` (344.674.486) across 9.173.764 km² (159.090 active 5-arcminute WGS84 pixels). Anchored to the inaugural 1790AD federal enumeration [@uscb1791], Bicentennial and Millennial historical census syntheses [@uscb1975; @carter2006], official 1910–2020AD state apportionment tables [@uscb2021apportion], annual 2000–2024AD subcounty resident estimates [@uscb2025subest] and territorial registers for Hawai'i, Bermuda and American Samoa [@schmitt1977; @bermuda2018; @uscb2022as], this module harmonises 53 jurisdictions onto fixed contemporary territorial masks.

Rural allocation beneath 36.949 catalogued settlements (38.969 candidate ledger records and 1.003.887 settlement-year observations) applies non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging surfaces calibrated across 93.129 North American archaeological site-period records (286.193 horizon records across 493.687 valid land cells and 3.833 domestic plus 251 buffer catchments; regularised $\tau_1 = 1,35$, mean short range 47,00 km, raw nugget 0, regularised 0,04, WLS $R^2 = 0,9990$ to 0,9992) and 20.670 domestic horizon site-epoch records in Hawai'i and American Samoa (282 valid and active cells, 156 domestic and 4 buffer catchments; matching raw and regularised $\tau_1$ averaging 1,0968 across 1,0673 to 1,1624, mean $\tau_2 = 2,3581$ across 2,2946 to 2,4991, range 5,44 km to 5,92 km [mean 5,59 km], raw nugget 0 and regularised 0,04 across all six horizons, WLS $R^2 = 0,9963$ to 0,9975) [@kelly2025].

Three structural shifts govern the 243-year trajectory. First, nineteenth-century trans-Appalachian and Great Plains settlement combined with mass transatlantic immigration to double national numbers roughly every twenty-five years until 1860AD [@easterlin1968; @haines2000]. Second, twentieth-century industrialisation concentrated growth in the Manufacturing Belt and Pacific coast before suburban dispersion and post-1965AD migration shifted gravity toward the Sunbelt [@frey2015; @balk2018understanding]. Third, the South Atlantic, West South Central and Mountain divisions expanded together from 27,02% (40,90M) of the national total in 1950AD to 41,38% (142,64M) in 2026AD.

# Background

## Continental Scale and Constitutional Enumeration (1783AD to 1860AD)

At the close of the Revolutionary War in 1783AD, Euro-American and enslaved African populations remained overwhelmingly confined between the Atlantic coast and the Appalachian crest, whilst Indigenous nations and Spanish-French garrisons held the Mississippi basin, Gulf coast, Great Plains, Southwest and Pacific slope [@uscb1975; @thornton1987]. The 1790AD First Federal Census enumerated 3,93M persons inside the early Union [@uscb1791]; adding unenumerated Indigenous inhabitants across western territories, Russian Alaska (60,4k) and Bermuda (10,2k) raises the composite 1790AD total across the 9,17M km² domain to 5.000.368 (Figure \ref{fig:hero-united-states-post-independence}).

Constitutional decennial apportionment mandated an unbroken series of counts every ten years from 1790AD onward, creating one of the longest continuous sub-national demographic records outside northwestern Europe [@carter2006; @uscb2021apportion]. Over the first seventy years after independence, federal territorial acquisitions, namely Louisiana (1803AD), Florida (1819AD), Texas (1845AD), Oregon (1846AD), the Mexican Cession (1848AD) and the Gadsden Purchase (1853AD), brought the entire contiguous temperate belt under a single census framework.

Demographic growth before 1860AD outpaced every contemporary European society. Early marriage, abundant frontier farmland and falling infant mortality sustained crude birth rates above forty per thousand well into the antebellum period [@easterlin1968; @haines2000]. From the 1830s onward, Irish famine refugees, German farmers and British artisans augmented high natural increase, lifting the composite total from 6,31M in 1800AD to 23,66M in 1850AD and 31,74M in 1860AD.

## Civil War Shock, Transcontinental Railways and Immigration Waves (1860AD to 1930AD)

Expansion across the 1860s slowed noticeably under the human cost of the American Civil War (1861–1865AD), which claimed approximately 750k military lives alongside civilian displacement and suppressed wartime births [@hacker2011; @haines2000]. Decennial growth dropped from 34,16% between 1850AD and 1860AD to 22,31% between 1860AD and 1870AD (31,74M to 38,82M), even after incorporating Alaska following its 1867AD purchase from Russia.

Between 1870AD and 1914AD, steel rails, refrigerated shipping and Great Plains barbed wire converted the Missouri-Mississippi grasslands into commercial grain and livestock country whilst industrial steel, coal and textile belts expanded across Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois and southern New England [@easterlin1968; @carter2006]. Successive European and Asian migration waves shifted from northwestern Europe toward southern and eastern Europe, raising the composite population from 50,44M in 1880AD to 76,24M in 1900AD and 106,05M in 1920AD.

At the same time, Indigenous demography reached its historical nadir around 1890–1900AD following Plains warfare, bison eradication, forced reservation confinement and infectious outbreaks, before twentieth-century public health and demographic recovery reversed centuries of post-contact contraction [@thornton1987]. Simultaneously, the 1898AD annexations of Hawai'i (135k at transfer) and American Samoa (5,7k in 1900AD) integrated central and South Pacific populations whose modern labour force soon reflected Asian and Polynesian migration [@schmitt1977; @uscb2022as].

## Fertility Transition, Depression Trough and Baby Boom (1920AD to 1970AD)

Quota acts in 1921AD and 1924AD curtailed transatlantic immigration abruptly, leaving national expansion dependent on domestic fertility and rural-to-urban migration [@easterlin1968]. During the 1930s Great Depression, delayed marriages and urban unemployment compressed fertility to historic lows, slowing national growth between 1930AD (123,24M) and 1940AD (132,21M) to 7,28% over the full decade whilst Dust Bowl drought displaced hundreds of thousands from Oklahoma, Kansas and the Dakotas toward California and the Pacific Northwest [@haines2000].

After 1945AD, economic expansion, veteran housing subsidies and suburban tract construction generated an unexpected eighteen-year baby boom lifting total population from 151,38M in 1950AD to 179,39M in 1960AD and 203,29M in 1970AD [@carter2006; @uscb1975]. During the same decades, Great Migration departures carried millions of Black and rural Southern workers northward and westward into Chicago, Detroit, New York, Philadelphia and Los Angeles before reverse return migration began during the 1970s [@dmowska2017comprehensive; @frey2015].

## Sunbelt Shift, Metropolitan Sprawl and Ageing (1970AD to 2026AD)

Following the 1965AD Immigration and Nationality Act, Latin American and Asian inflows replaced European immigration as the primary external demographic stream [@frey2015]. Meanwhile, residential air-conditioning, interstate freeways, defence procurement and corporate relocation reshaped internal geography: Rust Belt industrial cores in New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois and Michigan grew slowly or contracted locally while Florida, Texas, Georgia, North Carolina, Arizona and California expanded rapidly [@balk2018understanding; @uscb2025subest].

By the early twenty-first century, fertility fell below replacement across nearly all states, shifting policy and demographic attention toward regional population ageing [@wu2021spatiality], interregional migration sensitivity [@oizumi2022sensitivity], spatial segregation and gentrification legacies inside growing cities [@ibsen2025land; @dmowska2024quantification], and small-area migration probability estimation [@dyrting2024estimating]. Between 2000AD and 2026AD, net additions lifted the 53-jurisdiction total from 282,28M to 344,67M (22,1% cumulative growth), even as mortality shocks during 2020–2022AD briefly slowed annual gains [@uscb2025subest].

## Insular and Non-Contiguous Jurisdictions

Three geographically distinct territories round out the 53-jurisdiction domain. Alaska (1.420.613 km², 40.477 active cells) moved from 62,5k predominantly Aleut, Yupik, Inupiat, Athabascan and Tlingit inhabitants in 1783AD through Klondike and Nome mining booms (63,6k in 1900AD) and Cold War military-and-pipeline expansion (226,2k in 1960AD; 628k in 2000AD) to 743,7k in 2026AD [@uscb1975; @uscb2025subest].

Hawai'i (16.476 km², 278 pixels) enters the U.S. series at 1898AD annexation (135k), expanding through plantation labour, Pacific naval basing and postwar tourism to 499,8k in 1950AD and 1,44M in 2026AD [@schmitt1977; @uscb2025subest]. American Samoa (124 km² across 4 active 5-arcminute pixels) rose from 5.679 in 1900AD to 57.291 in 2000AD before out-migration to Hawai'i and the U.S. mainland trimmed its 2026AD population to 46.500 [@uscb2022as], while Bermuda (53 km² across 1 active pixel) rose continuously from 10.381 in 1783AD to 64.750 in 2026AD [@bermuda2018].

# Methodology

## State Mask Harmonisation and Pre-Statehood Continuity

All 53 territorial series map onto fixed modern state and territory polygons on CENTAUR-II's shared 5-arcminute WGS84 terrestrial grid (159.090 active pixels). Four cross-module rules govern historical boundaries without artificial step jumps:

1. **Colonial-to-Independence Seam (1783AD)**: Initial 1783AD state benchmarks (4.375.088 headline; 4.376.370 across active state polygons) reconcile against the 4.074.302 terminal total of the 1754–1783AD colonial America synthesis after adding Alaska (62.500), Bermuda (10.381), western Indigenous groups and early frontier alignments. Future states carved out of parent eastern polities, notably Vermont (1791AD), Kentucky (1792AD), Tennessee (1796AD), Maine (1820AD from Massachusetts) and West Virginia (1863AD from Virginia), receive continuous backward estimates onto their modern polygons from 1783AD onward [@uscb1975; @carter2006].
2. **Retroceded and Adjusted Eastern Boundaries**: Settlements affected by the 1846–1847AD Virginia retrocession (Alexandria and Arlington returned from the District of Columbia to Virginia) and the 1862AD Massachusetts-Rhode Island border adjustment (Pawtucket and East Providence transferred to Rhode Island alongside Fall River and Seekonk in Massachusetts) align consistently to modern state masks, while pre-1871AD Georgetown merges cleanly into Washington.
3. **Pacific Annexation Handover (1898–1900AD)**: Hawai'i (135.000 in 1898AD) and American Samoa (5.679 in 1900AD) enter strictly at annexation, leaving pre-1898AD Polynesian demography inside the dedicated pre-annexation Hawaiian and Polynesian module [@schmitt1977; @uscb2022as].
4. **Alaska and Bermuda Continuity**: Alaska bridges from pre-1867AD Russian-and-Indigenous population estimates (62.500 in 1783AD; 33.426 at the inaugural 1880AD U.S. census) directly into decennial federal enumerations, while Bermuda tracks colonial and Bermudian census benchmarks (10.381 in 1783AD to 64.750 in 2026AD) [@bermuda2018].

## Census Ingestion, Subcounty Estimates and Uncertainty Envelopes

From 1790AD to 1900AD, decennial state totals draw directly on federal census schedules and Historical Statistics reconstructions [@uscb1791; @uscb1975; @carter2006]. From 1910AD to 2020AD, official decennial apportionment totals [@uscb2021apportion] merge with 2000–2024AD Census Bureau intercensal and post-censal resident estimates [@uscb2025subest], retaining annual post-2000AD trajectories across every state and the District of Columbia. State populations for 2025AD and 2026AD project each jurisdiction's 2020–2024AD compound annual growth rate clamped strictly inside [0,98; 1,03].

Every regional benchmark carries symmetric ±1,5% uncertainty intervals to accommodate census net undercoverage, historically higher in frontier counties, minority neighbourhoods and unenumerated rural tracts, and synthetic cohort adjustment [@banda2015impact; @namazirad2014generating]. Where subcounty urban-settlement totals in dense nineteenth- and twentieth-century industrial states (New York, Illinois, Massachusetts) exceed raw municipal baselines due to co-located townships and census towns, state trajectories incorporate an urban-reconciliation floor so pixel subtraction never yields negative rural densities (Table \ref{tab:us-divisions}).

## Urban Subtraction and Dual-Domain Matérn Kriging

To prevent nineteenth-century frontier towns or modern suburban tracts from distorting rural distributions, urban and rural strata are allocated separately. First, 36.949 catalogued settlements (1.003.887 place-year observations) disaggregate onto urban cells using statutory incorporated places (SUMLEV 162), consolidated governments (SUMLEV 170), Census-Designated Places (CDPs) and non-overlapping Minor Civil Divisions (SUMLEV 060) across New England and the Mid-Atlantic [@uscb2025subest; @balk2018understanding]. Post-1898AD consolidated New York City boroughs (Manhattan, The Bronx, Queens, Staten Island) remain unified inside Greater New York (New York-New York, with pre-1898 constituent series carried for The Bronx, Queens and Staten Island), keeping urban subtraction exact without double-counting Manhattan.

Residual rural population inside the 158.808 mainland, Alaskan and Bermudian cells is distributed using the North American non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging surface calibrated across 493.687 valid terrestrial cells (18.561.382 km² or 18,56M km², with 78.938 to 149.138 active cells across 10 horizons 13000BC to 1650AD) and 93.129 unique archaeological site-period observations (286.193 horizon site records across 3.833 domestic catchments covering 15.517.268 km² or 15,52M km², 2.570 active or 67,05%, equivalent circular radius median 29,48 km and 90th percentile 40,95 km overall [29,3 km and 39,85 km active; diagnostic Voronoi radius 29,78 km and 40,69 km], 14,24x the 6.539-entry legacy radiocarbon baseline, plus 251 cross-frontier buffer catchments up to 300 km into Northern Mexico, Chukotka and Caribbean neighbours) [@kelly2025]. Across all ten horizons (13000BC to 1650AD; Table \ref{tab:us-kriging}), the continental surface achieves regularised dimensionless short range $\tau_1 = 1,35$ across all ten horizons (raw 1,519 to 1,6098, horizon mean 1,5782), macro range $\tau_2 = 2,9025$ (2,9), effective short range 45,23 to 47,94 km (mean 47,00 km), raw nugget-to-sill ratio 0 across all ten horizons (regularised 0,04, $\eta = 0,0417$) and WLS residual $R^2$ from 0,9990 to 0,9992 (mean 0,9991).

Across the 282 valid and active 5-arcminute pixels of Hawai'i (278) and American Samoa (4), a dedicated six-horizon kriging surface conditions 20.670 domestic horizon site-epoch records partitioned across 156 domestic catchments (156 active, plus 4 Samoan buffer catchments) derived from 727 State of Hawai'i *ahupua'a* land divisions (median radius 4,92 km, 90th percentile 8,29 km; matching raw and regularised $\tau_1$ averaging 1,0968 [1,0673 to 1,1624]; mean $\tau_2 = 2,3581$ [2,2946 to 2,4991]; effective short range 5,44 to 5,92 km, mean 5,59 km; raw nugget-to-sill ratio 0 and regularised 0,04 [$\eta = 0,0417$] across all six horizons, WLS $R^2$ 0,9963 to 0,9975). Two passes of a 5-pixel separable log-multiplier filter with four-pixel border feathering then smooth residual rural transitions across state lines, riverine boundaries and international borders while holding every state sum exact.

# Testing and Validation

Four validation checks confirm apportionment reconciliation, gazetteer balance, Pacific handover isolation and kriging calibration across all 53 jurisdictions.

## Apportionment and Subcounty Reconciliation

Annual state totals from 2000AD to 2024AD match U.S. Census Bureau resident series directly [@uscb2025subest], while 1910–2020AD decennial state anchors match official apportionment returns [@uscb2021apportion]. Pre-1910AD state and territorial figures reconcile against Historical Statistics Series A 195-209 [@uscb1975; @carter2006] without double-counting partitioned states (Maine, West Virginia) or unorganised western territories.

## Gazetteer and Ledger Balance

Cross-checking 36.949 included settlements (1.003.887 place-year observations; 36.739 settlements with >= 3 chronological entries and continuous pre-1975AD historical trajectories) against 2.020 excluded ledger candidates confirms 38.969 total candidates with zero unaccounted entries. Exclusions comprise 2.014 subordinate suburbs merged within 1,55 km of canonical centres, 3 out-of-bounds Caribbean and Micronesian territories (San Juan, Charlotte Amalie, Hagåtña) assigned to neighbouring macro-regions and 3 alias duplicates (District of Columbia unified under Washington, Manhattan under pre-consolidation New York-New York, and New Boston-Morea under Morea in Pennsylvania).

## Pacific Handover and Kriging Calibration

Hawai'i (167 catalogued settlements, led by Honolulu) and American Samoa (29 village entries starting from 1970AD) connect cleanly to the pre-1898AD Polynesian baseline, with Hawai'i entering the regional manifest at 1898AD (135.000) and American Samoa at 1900AD (5.679) (Table \ref{tab:us-divisions}). Both the continental and central Pacific kriging surfaces satisfy sharpness tolerances (regularised $\tau_1 = 1,35 \le 1,8$ across all ten horizons 13000BC to 1650AD, raw 1,519 to 1,6098 with horizon mean 1,5782 in North America; matching raw and regularised $\tau_1$ averaging 1,0968 $\le 1,8$ across 1,0673 to 1,1624 in Hawai'i and Polynesia; raw nugget 0 and regularised nugget-to-sill ratio 0,04 [$\eta = 0,0417$] across all ten horizons in North America and all six horizons in Hawai'i and Polynesia, all < 0,45; Table \ref{tab:us-kriging}).

```{r tbl-us-kriging, results='asis'}
na_labels <- c(
  palaeoindian_early_archaic = "NA: Palaeoindian and Early Archaic",
  late_archaic = "NA: Late Archaic",
  middle_woodland_hopewell = "NA: Middle Woodland (Hopewell)",
  middle_mississippian_pueblo_iii = "NA: Middle Mississippian (Pueblo III)",
  protohistoric_contact_horizon = "NA: Protohistoric Contact Horizon"
)
hp_labels <- c(
  colonisation_founder = "Pacific: Colonisation Founder",
  dryland_intensification = "Pacific: Dryland Intensification",
  protohistoric_archaic_state = "Pacific: Protohistoric Archaic State",
  late_kingdom_plantation = "Pacific: Late Kingdom and Plantation"
)
rows_k <- c(
  lapply(names(na_labels), function (h) {
    v <- diag_na$variogram_models[[h]]
    s <- diag_na$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]
    data.frame(
      Horizon = unname(na_labels[h]),
      RangeKm = viscount_fmt_number(v$effective_short_range_km, 2L),
      Tau1 = viscount_fmt_number(v$raw_tau1_dimensionless, 4L),
      RegNugget = viscount_fmt_number(v$nugget_to_sill_ratio, 4L),
      MeanDens = viscount_fmt_number(s$mean_value, 4L),
      ResidualR2 = viscount_fmt_number(v$residual_r2, 4L),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }),
  lapply(names(hp_labels), function (h) {
    v <- diag_hp$variogram_models[[h]]
    s <- diag_hp$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]
    data.frame(
      Horizon = unname(hp_labels[h]),
      RangeKm = viscount_fmt_number(v$effective_short_range_km, 2L),
      Tau1 = viscount_fmt_number(v$raw_tau1_dimensionless, 4L),
      RegNugget = viscount_fmt_number(v$nugget_to_sill_ratio, 4L),
      MeanDens = viscount_fmt_number(s$mean_value, 4L),
      ResidualR2 = viscount_fmt_number(v$residual_r2, 4L),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })
)
df_us_k <- do.call(rbind, rows_k)
rownames(df_us_k) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_us_k,
  "Representative North American (NA) and Hawaiian-Samoan (Pacific) non-stationary Matérn kriging calibration horizons.",
  c("Domain and Horizon", "Range (km)", "Raw Tau 1", "Reg. Nugget", "Mean Density", "Residual R²"),
  list(label = "tab:us-kriging", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

  Division = div_names,
  Area = vapply(div_names, function (d) viscount_fmt_number(sum(vapply(divs[[d]], function (k) us_mod$regions[[k]]$area_km2, numeric(1))), 0L), character(1)),

  P1950 = vapply(div_names, function (d) viscount_fmt_pop(sum_div(divs[[d]], 1950)), character(1)),
  P2000 = vapply(div_names, function (d) viscount_fmt_pop(sum_div(divs[[d]], 2000)), character(1)),
  P2026 = vapply(div_names, function (d) viscount_fmt_pop(sum_div(divs[[d]], 2026)), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_div <- rbind(df_div, data.frame(
  Division = "Composite Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(us_mod$total_area_km2, 0L),
  P1783 = viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["1783"]]),
  P1850 = viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["1850"]]),

))
rownames(df_div) <- NULL

viscount_table(

  c("Division", "Area (km²)", "1783AD", "1850AD", "1900AD", "1950AD", "2000AD", "2026AD"),

)

# Results

## Continental Transition and Regional Divergence (1783AD to 1950AD)

Across 243 years (Figure \ref{fig:us-trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:us-divisions}), headline population rose from 4,38M in 1783AD to 23,66M in 1850AD, 76,24M in 1900AD, 151,38M in 1950AD and 344,67M in 2026AD. At independence in 1783AD, the eastern seaboard held 73,82% of the composite total (1,58M in South Atlantic, 847,9k in New England and 805,3k in Middle Atlantic), led by Virginia (581,1k in 1783AD; 691,7k in 1790AD), Pennsylvania (364,9k; 434,4k), North Carolina (330,8k; 393,8k) and Massachusetts (318,2k; 378,8k) [@uscb1791].

By 1850AD, Erie Canal trade, steamboats on the Ohio-Mississippi system and early trunk railroads had shifted the demographic centre into Middle Atlantic (6,51M) and East North Central (4,52M). New York (3,64M in 1850AD; 4,55M in 1860AD) held first place among states from 1810AD until overtaken by California during the 1960s (10,59M vs 15,46M in 1950AD; 15,72M vs 17,12M in 1960AD; 19,95M vs 18,53M in 1970AD) [@carter2006].

By 1900AD, East North Central (15,99M) and Middle Atlantic (15,83M) together accounted for 41,73% of the national total, whilst West North Central climbed to 10,35M following homestead settlement across Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Kansas and Nebraska [@haines2000]. Over the next half-century, industrial employment concentrated across the Great Lakes and Mid-Atlantic even as California's oil, cinema, shipbuilding and wartime aerospace industries expanded the Pacific division from 2,63M in 1900AD to 15,11M in 1950AD.

```{r fig-us-shares, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_united_states_post_independence_shares.png",
  "Long-run shifts in state demographic shares across the United States, Bermuda and American Samoa (1783AD to 2026AD).",
  "fig:us-shares"
)
```

## Sunbelt and Pacific Rebalancing (1950AD to 2026AD)

After 1950AD, residential cooling, interstate highways, federal military-industrial dispersal and suburban Sunbelt job formation reversed a century and a half of northern concentration (Figure \ref{fig:us-shares} and Table \ref{tab:us-top-states}). Between 1950AD and 2026AD, the South Atlantic division more than tripled from 21,28M to 71,64M (20,78% of headline population), paced by Florida (2,77M to 24,32M), Georgia (3,44M to 11,41M), North Carolina (4,06M to 11,36M) and Virginia (3,32M to 8,9M) [@frey2015; @uscb2025subest].

West South Central rose equally sharply from 14,54M in 1950AD to 44,23M in 2026AD as Texas surged more than fourfold from 7,71M to 32,37M, while Mountain states multiplied more than fivefold from 5,07M to 26,77M led by Arizona (749,6k to 7,79M), Colorado and Utah. Together, South Atlantic, West South Central and Mountain rose from 27,02% of composite headline population in 1950AD to 41,38% in 2026AD.

California peaked at 39,52M in 2020AD (39,39M in 2026AD), yet domestic out-migration tempered Pacific growth after 2010AD while New York (19,75M in 2026AD, down from 20,99M in 2000AD and 21,54M in 2010AD), Illinois (12,67M, down from 12,87M in 2000AD and 13,17M in 2010AD) and Pennsylvania (13,12M) grew far more modestly or stabilised [@uscb2025subest; @dmowska2024quantification]. In the insular jurisdictions, Hawai'i rose from 135k at 1898AD annexation to 1,44M in 2026AD, Bermuda grew from 10.381 in 1783AD to 64.750 in 2026AD and American Samoa rose from 5.679 in 1900AD to 57.291 in 2000AD before settling near 46.500 in 2026AD [@schmitt1977; @bermuda2018; @uscb2022as].

```{r tbl-us-top-states, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(us_mod$regions)
p26_all <- vapply(reg_keys, function (k) interp_reg(us_mod$regions[[k]], 2026), numeric(1))
top12_keys <- reg_keys[order(p26_all, decreasing = TRUE)[1:12]]

df_top12 <- data.frame(
  State = vapply(top12_keys, function (k) sub("^\\d+\\.\\s*", "", us_mod$regions[[k]]$name), character(1)),
  Area = vapply(top12_keys, function (k) viscount_fmt_number(us_mod$regions[[k]]$area_km2, 0L), character(1)),
  P1783 = vapply(top12_keys, function (k) viscount_fmt_pop(interp_reg(us_mod$regions[[k]], 1783)), character(1)),
  P1860 = vapply(top12_keys, function (k) viscount_fmt_pop(interp_reg(us_mod$regions[[k]], 1860)), character(1)),
  P1900 = vapply(top12_keys, function (k) viscount_fmt_pop(interp_reg(us_mod$regions[[k]], 1900)), character(1)),
  P1950 = vapply(top12_keys, function (k) viscount_fmt_pop(interp_reg(us_mod$regions[[k]], 1950)), character(1)),
  P2000 = vapply(top12_keys, function (k) viscount_fmt_pop(interp_reg(us_mod$regions[[k]], 2000)), character(1)),
  P2026 = vapply(top12_keys, function (k) viscount_fmt_pop(interp_reg(us_mod$regions[[k]], 2026)), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_top12) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_top12,
  "Long-run trajectories of the twelve most populous U.S. states in 2026AD (1783AD to 2026AD).",
  c("State", "Area (km²)", "1783AD", "1860AD", "1900AD", "1950AD", "2000AD", "2026AD"),
  list(label = "tab:us-top-states")
)
```

## Urbanisation, Rural Depopulation and Internal Migration Dynamics

Behind state-level shifts lay an uninterrupted rural-to-urban transition across 36.949 catalogued towns, cities, Minor Civil Divisions and Census-Designated Places (Table \ref{tab:us-benchmarks}). Catalogued settlement totals climbed from 16,28% of the regional total in 1790AD (814,1k across 590 places) and 44,21% in 1850AD (10,46M) to 53,86% in 1900AD (41,06M), 73,20% in 1950AD (110,80M) and 82,98% in 2000AD (234,23M).

After 1950AD, metropolitan expansion shifted away from dense core cities toward sprawling outer counties and Census-Designated Places, a transition traced directly across satellite-derived urban classes and census tracts [@balk2018understanding; @ibsen2025land]. Great Plains rural counties across North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas and Iowa lost farm cohorts for decades as agricultural mechanisation concentrated young workers in regional hubs such as Fargo, Omaha, Des Moines and Kansas City [@haines2000; @dyrting2024estimating].

```{r tbl-us-benchmarks, results='asis'}
us_b_yrs <- c("1783", "1790", "1820", "1850", "1880", "1900", "1920", "1940", "1950", "1960", "1970", "1980", "1990", "2000", "2010", "2020", "2026")
us_b_pops <- vapply(us_b_yrs, function (y) as.numeric(hl[[y]]), numeric(1))
us_b_cagr <- c("-", vapply(seq_along(us_b_yrs)[-1], function (idx) {
  dt <- as.integer(us_b_yrs[idx]) - as.integer(us_b_yrs[idx - 1L])
  r <- 100 * ((us_b_pops[idx] / us_b_pops[idx - 1L])^(1 / dt) - 1)
  paste0(viscount_fmt_number(r, 2L), "%")
}, character(1)))
us_b_cnt <- vapply(us_b_yrs, function (y) {
  viscount_fmt_number(sum(vapply(us_sett, function (x) !is.null(x$population[[y]]), logical(1))), 0L)
}, character(1))
us_b_sum <- vapply(us_b_yrs, function (y) {
  s <- sum(vapply(us_sett, function (x) {
    v <- x$population[[y]]
    if (is.null(v)) 0 else as.numeric(v)
  }, numeric(1)))
  viscount_fmt_pop(s)
}, character(1))
df_us_b <- data.frame(
  Year = paste0(us_b_yrs, "AD"),
  Total = vapply(us_b_pops, viscount_fmt_pop, character(1)),
  Exact = vapply(us_b_pops, function (v) viscount_fmt_number(v, 0L), character(1)),
  Growth = us_b_cagr,
  Places = us_b_cnt,
  UrbanSum = us_b_sum,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_us_b) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_us_b,
  "Benchmark population series, annual interval growth rates and catalogued settlement sums across the United States, Bermuda and American Samoa (1783AD to 2026AD).",
  c("Year", "Total", "Exact Count", "Annual Growth", "Places", "Settlement Sum"),
  list(label = "tab:us-benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Meanwhile, demographic ageing across New England, the Upper Midwest and rural Appalachia contrasted sharply with youthful demographic profiles across Utah, Texas and immigrant-receiving Sunbelt corridors [@wu2021spatiality; @oizumi2022sensitivity]. Comparative fertility and vital-registration analyses confirm how strongly household age structure, internal migration and local public-health access interact with regional urbanisation [@salam2015components; @hosseini2021between; @dhole2025coverage].

Across the nine geographic divisions (Table \ref{tab:us-divisions}), long-run density diverged markedly between eastern metropolises and western basins. By 2026AD, Middle Atlantic (42,49M across 259.647 km², or 163,63 persons per km²) and New England (15,55M across 164.496 km², or 94,55 persons per km²) remained densely settled despite slow growth, whereas Mountain (26,77M across 2.234.493 km², or 11,98 persons per km²) and West North Central (22,16M across 1.325.003 km², or 16,72 persons per km²) stayed overwhelmingly concentrated in metropolitan oases and river corridors.

Within individual states, spatial concentration produced striking internal contrasts (Table \ref{tab:us-top-states}). Nevada grew from sparse mining camps in 1860AD into a state of more than 3M inhabitants anchored predominantly around Las Vegas and Reno, whilst Florida rose from 140,4k in 1860AD to 24,32M in 2026AD (169,07 persons per km²) following mosquito eradication, coastal drainage, tourism and retiree settlement [@frey2015].

# Limitations

Five structural constraints apply to the 1783AD to 2026AD series. First, pre-statehood 1783AD figures across trans-Appalachian, Plains and western masks blend sparse archaeological carrying-capacity baselines with colonial garrison estimates, yielding wider uncertainty prior to formal federal census enumeration [@thornton1987; @uscb1975].

Second, pre-2000AD benchmarks rest on decennial census dates rather than annual vital accounts, smoothing over sharp intra-decade shocks including the 1861–1865AD Civil War losses [@hacker2011], the 1918–1919AD influenza pandemic and 1930s Dust Bowl out-migration.

Third, projecting nineteenth-century censuses onto modern state masks assigns antebellum Maine (prior to 1820AD), West Virginia (prior to 1863AD) and Dakota Territory sub-districts directly to modern polygons rather than tracing shifting antebellum territorial boundaries. Similarly, reconciling dense city-proper sums with state totals elevates regional series slightly above decennial state totals in New York and Illinois where historic townships coexist with urban centres.

Fourth, rural spatial weighting derives from Holocene radiocarbon and *ahupua'a* catchments combined with coastal, fluvial and terrain covariates; whilst these weights distribute rural populations accurately along settled river valleys and coasts, twentieth-century irrigated desert farming and suburban highway corridors rely principally on explicit CDP and incorporated-place ingestion rather than prehistoric settlement priors.

Fifth, 2025AD and 2026AD state entries project 2020–2024AD Census Bureau post-censal trends clamped to [0,98; 1,03], remaining provisional until the 2030AD decennial census [@uscb2025subest]. On the 5-arcminute grid, micro-atolls in American Samoa and Bermudian parishes span only one to four ocean-bounded pixels, heightening per-pixel sensitivity relative to large continental states.

# Conclusion

Between 1783AD and 2026AD, the United States, Bermuda and post-1898AD American Samoa grew from a 4,38M Atlantic republic into a continental-and-Pacific system of 344,67M inhabitants across 9,17M km². Harmonising 53 territorial masks, federal apportionment counts, annual subcounty estimates and 36.949 geolocated settlements (38.969 ledger candidates and 1.003.887 observations) eliminates nineteenth-century territorial step artefacts whilst capturing both the rise of the Manufacturing Belt and the post-1950AD Sunbelt shift.

Coupled with dual-domain non-stationary Matérn kriging ($\tau_1 = 1,35$, mean short range 47,00 km and regularised nugget 0,04 across 93.129 North American site-periods; matching raw and regularised mean $\tau_1 = 1,0968$, mean short range 5,59 km and regularised nugget 0,04 across 20.670 domestic horizon site-epoch records in Hawai'i and American Samoa), the dataset connects colonial demography directly with twenty-first-century subcounty geography across every state, division and island territory.

Future decennial census releases from 2030AD onward and ongoing digitisation of nineteenth-century territorial manuscript schedules can slot straight into these fixed 53 territorial masks without altering historical benchmarks or cross-border smoothing rules. By keeping statutory incorporated places, non-overlapping Minor Civil Divisions and residual rural surfaces cleanly separated, the reconstruction provides a consistent demographic series across two and a half centuries of continental change.
